question: A synthesis-stage coordinator combines findings from six research subagents into a final report. Two subagents lost access to their assigned sources partway through. Which output structure best communicates the reliability of the final report to a downstream reader?
options: A) Append one generic disclaimer noting that some unspecified sources may have been unavailable overall
B) Annotate coverage so readers see which sections are well-supported by completed sources and which have gaps
C) Omit the two affected sections entirely so the reader only sees content from fully successful subagents
D) Present all findings as one uniform narrative with no distinction between complete and partial-source sections
correct_answers: B) Annotate coverage so readers see which sections are well-supported by completed sources and which have gaps
explanations: A generic, non-specific disclaimer doesn't tell the reader which sections are affected, so they cannot judge which claims to trust less.
Correct. Coverage annotations let the reader see exactly which claims rest on solid evidence and which areas are thin because of source access problems, preserving both value and honesty.
Dropping the affected sections silently removes information the reader might still find useful and hides that a gap exists at all.
A uniform narrative with no distinction implies every section has equal evidentiary support, which misrepresents the sections affected by the access failures.
